item.content:encoded:
The 39 th Guam Legislature will bring new faces, as well as some returning senators, into Guam’s lawmaking body.

A number of senators in the 38 th Guam Legislature gave up their seats to run for higher office. Republican Speaker Frank Blas Jr., Republican Vice Speaker Tony Ada and Democratic Sens. Therese Terlaje and Joe San Agustin all ran for governor, with Ada winning the island’s highest office.

Democratic Sens. Sabina Perez and Tina Muna Barnes ran for lieutenant governor.

That left nine incumbents, all of whom won reelection.

They are Republicans Sabrina Salas Matanane, Jesse Lujan, Chris Duenas, Shelly Calvo, Telo Taitague, Vincent Borja and Eulogio Shawn Gumatatao. Democratic incumbents reelected were Chris Barnett and William Parkinson.

Former Democratic Sens. Amanda Shelton, Telena Nelson and Clynton Ridgell were elected Tuesday, along with Democratic legislative newcomers Donna Quinata and Kallen Perez.

Hoa Nyugen is the Republican newcomer, giving the party an 8-7 majority in the 39 th Legislature.

item.content:encoded:
The Department of Public Health and Social Services will conduct a village outreach program in Chalan Pago-Ordot on Nov. 6.

The event runs from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the Chalan Pago-Ordot Multipurpose Emergency Center. Residents can learn about several Public Health programs, get help with applications, and learn about available community resources.

Immunizations will be available for children ages 2 months to 18 years who are enrolled in Medicaid or the Medically Indigent Program or who have no health insurance.

Parents must bring the child’s birth certificate, current immunization record, and their own valid photo ID. Children must be accompanied by a parent or have written authorization or legal documentation allowing another adult to accompany them.

Public Health will also provide educational information on diabetes, tobacco, lead exposure, and hypertension. The Bureau of Child Care Services will have child care assistance applications and program materials available.

Residents can also receive eligibility assessments for the Breast Cervical Cancer Screening Program and the Women, Infants, and Children program. Information will also be available on mental health and primary care services, the aging program, and Adult Protective Services.

Public Health says this is its first village outreach event for fiscal year 2027, part of an effort to make health and social services more accessible to residents.

The department notes that tuberculosis skin tests, also known as PPD tests, will not be offered for the outreach program.

item.title: King-Hinds wins reelection in landslide; Governor, AG races head to runoff
item.description: Republican incumbent Kimberlyn King-Hinds won reelection Tuesday as the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands' delegate to the U.S. House of Representatives, capturing nearly two-thirds of the vote in a decisive victory that highlighted the 2026 general election. Unofficial results showed King-Hinds receiving 8,194 votes, or 63.7% of ballots cast in the delegate race, securing another two-y
item.content:encoded:
Republican incumbent Kimberlyn King-Hinds won reelection Tuesday as the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands' delegate to the U.S. House of Representatives, capturing nearly two-thirds of the vote in a decisive victory that highlighted the 2026 general election.

Unofficial results showed King-Hinds receiving 8,194 votes, or 63.7% of ballots cast in the delegate race, securing another two-year term in Congress. Independent challenger Galvin Sablan Deleon Guerrero garnered 4,675 votes, or 36%.

While the delegate race produced a clear winner, voters left the contests for governor and attorney general unsettled, triggering runoff elections under CNMI law.

The Republican gubernatorial ticket of Ralph DLG Torres and Benjamin Jones Jr. finished first but failed to capture a majority of votes cast. They will face the independent team of Blas Jonathan Attao and Edmund S. Villagomez in a runoff election.

The independent ticket of Lawrence Camacho and Edith E. Deleon Guerrero finished third and was eliminated from contention.

In the attorney general race, attorneys Joaquin DLG Torres and Michael Evangelista advanced to a runoff after neither candidate secured more than 50% of the vote. Attorney Jonathan Robert Glass Jr. placed third.

The race for attorney general was among the night's closest contests. Evangelista edged Glass by only 18 votes to claim the second runoff spot and keep his campaign alive.

Under CNMI law, a runoff election is required when no gubernatorial ticket or attorney general candidate receives more than half of all votes cast and counted in the general election. The runoff must be held within 14 days after the Commonwealth Election Commission certifies the election results.

Voters also considered whether to convene a constitutional convention to propose amendments to the CNMI Constitution. The proposal received majority support, with 7,602 voters casting ballots in favor and 4,324 voting against.

However, the measure failed because it did not meet the constitutional requirement that at least two-thirds of all votes cast on the question commonwealthwide be in favor. As a result, no constitutional convention will be convened.

The results set up two weeks of campaigning before voters return to the polls to decide the governor's office and attorney general post, while King-Hinds prepares to serve another term as the CNMI's representative in Washington.

item.title: Democrats win full control of Congress, ushering in a new era of divided government
item.description: Updated November 4, 2026 at 4:12 PM ChST Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 4, 2026 at 4:12 PM ChST

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democrats have cemented control of both chambers of Congress, according to an NPR analysis based on a tally of race calls by The Associated Press.

The twin victories in the House and Senate return the Democratic Party to full control of Congress for the first time since 2023 and deepens the level of expected friction between President Trump and congressional Democrats in a new era of divided government. After a largely unrestrained start to his second term, Trump's final two years in the White House are now certain to be hampered by congressional investigations in two chambers and legislators hostile to his agenda.

The midterm campaign was defined by Americans' frustrations with the high cost of living and perceived public corruption. Those concerns were at the heart of Democratic campaign messaging, including in the seven Senate races that flipped from Republican control: North Carolina , South Carolina , Ohio , Texas , Kansas , Iowa and Maine . Democrats also easily held onto a Senate seat in Georgia, despite its swing-state status.

In the House, Democrats secured a number of flips in key races, including at least three Florida districts that the state's Republican legislature redrew in an effort to stymie Democratic candidates. Democratic candidates also managed to oust four Republican incumbents in swing districts across Pennsylvania, all of that state's competitive races.

"From sea to shining sea, the American people have spoken and made clear they've had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption," said Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat who is poised to become the next Speaker of the House. "They want a Congress that's going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January."

Now, Washington enters a new political moment. Come January, when the new Congress is sworn in, President Trump is certain to face an onslaught of investigations and congressional oversight. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., expected to become chair of the House Oversight committee, did not mince words in the statement he posted to X: "LAWYER UP."

Still, voters hoping to see swift policy change could be disappointed. Trump retains his veto power, meaning legislation passed by Congress will almost certainly need his support to become law. That means Democrats' affordability-focused agenda may ultimately become a messaging tool for the 2028 election season, rather than a near-term policy intervention in Americans' everyday lives.

In an interview with the Pod Force One podcast that was published Monday, Trump addressed the prospect of losing unified Republican control in Washington, saying he would block Democrats' legislation if they take control of Congress.

"I'll become Mr. Veto," Trump said, adding, "and then at some point we'll probably make deals."

Democrats will have to work with Republicans on some must-pass legislation, including the 12 annual appropriations bills needed to fund the government.

Still, the party's control of the Senate will halt the steady confirmation of Trump-nominated judges through the body. It also means that any Cabinet nominees will need the support of at least a handful of Democrats to take the posts in a permanent capacity.

When it comes to investigations, Democrats have signaled an ambitious agenda, with potential inquiries into everything from the independence of agencies such as the Justice Department and Homeland Security, to the business interests of the president and his family.

The Senate win marked a long-fought victory for Democrats, and an electoral disaster for Republicans, who began the year with little expectation that their 53–47 majority was at risk. But with voters frustrated about the cost of living, the GOP was forced to compete in several states that President Trump won by double digits in 2024.

By early Wednesday morning, House Democrats had secured wins in seats that long seemed to be surefire Republican districts. In Kentucky, Democrats picked up a Lexington-area district that President Trump won with 57% of the vote in 2024.

Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Ala., will also be returning to Congress. His district in Alabama's Black Belt was redrawn to heavily favor Republicans after the Supreme Court's conservative supermajority dismantled key provisions of the Voting Rights Act.

In the closing weeks of the election, President Trump took to the campaign trail and implored Republican voters to pretend he was on the ballot. But at a moment when Trump's approval ratings are hovering at historic lows, below 40 percent, the argument was not enough to save the GOP majority.

Losing the Senate majority marks a blow for Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D.

In a post to X early Wednesday morning, Thune said that "Senate Republicans have put up a strong record of accomplishment that's created safer streets, more money in Americans' pockets, and new opportunities for families and businesses to get ahead."

"I'm proud of our team and everything we've done for the American people," Thune wrote. "Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we've done"

Across the aisle, Democrats' victory represents a vindication for Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who faced criticism from some progressives early in the president's second term that he was not doing enough to stand up to Trump.

In an October floor speech, Schumer said Democrats were ready to challenge President Trump and Republicans' agenda.

"We are ready to hit the ground running to lower costs, rein in chaos and stop the corruption," Schumer said. "Republicans broke faith with the American people. We know we need to build that trust with the Americans back up, and we will."

item.title: Democrat Josh Turek wins the Senate seat in Iowa
item.description: Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app Democrat Josh Turek has won the U.S. Senate race in Iowa, according to a race call by The Associated Press. His win ends more than a decade of Republican control of both Senate seats in the state.
item.content:encoded:
Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democrat Josh Turek has won the U.S. Senate race in Iowa, according to a race call by The Associated Press. His win ends more than a decade of Republican control of both Senate seats in the state.

Turek, a state representative from Council Bluffs, beat Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinson. He flipped one of the country's most competitive U.S. Senate seats, replacing retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst, who announced she would not be seeking a third term last fall.

Turek is a two-time gold medalist playing basketball in the Paralympics. He uses a wheelchair due to spina bifida, a condition he says is due to his father's exposure to Agent Orange in the Vietnam War. He was a relatively unknown state lawmaker who beat Zach Wahls, the former state Senate minority leader, to get the Democratic nomination in June.

Turek, who calls himself a "prairie populist," campaigned hard on healthcare reform, attacking Hinson for her support of Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which reduces Medicaid spending nationwide by nearly $1 trillion , and claims that Hinson's personal wealth has increased significantly during her time in Washington .

Both Hinson and Turek emphasized their ability as bipartisan lawmakers to try to sway the state's large number of uncommitted voters, but increased their attacks against their opponents, especially as polling data started to indicate a close race.

As President Trump's approval ratings fell, Iowa's race became more competitive. The state's large agricultural industry in particular has been hit hard by Trump's tariffs and increased diesel prices due to the war in Iran. Hinson seemed to walk a fine line with voters, as some Republicans running for office started distancing themselves from Trump. By summer, the race was considered a toss-up.

The race was one of the most expensive in the country. Federal spending data shows that together, the candidates raised more than $30 million. Outside groups contributed more than $100 million to the race, according to Open Secrets.

In the final quarter of the election, Turek significantly outraised his opponent Hinson, a former TV journalist who was considered a rising star in Iowa politics. Hinson was initially considered a front-runner to replace Ernst and received President Trump's endorsement shortly after she announced her candidacy in a state that has voted for President Trump three times. Trump carried Iowa by a 13-point margin in 2024.
